screens.title: Auditing Blockchain Systems and Smart Contracts
screens.narratorSegment: Auditing smart contracts and blockchain systems is not an optional step; it's a fundamental safety practice. In an immutable environment, bugs become permanent unless you design costly migrations, so catching issues early protects funds, users, and reputation. In this lesson you will learn the three primary audit methodologies — manual review, automated scanning, and formal verification — how audits are staged from scoping to re-audit, and the common vulnerability patterns auditors look for. We'll connect these methods to concrete historical examples, like reentrancy and access-control errors, so you can see how a small flaw produced outsized loss. You will also get a practical orientation to running a static analyzer on a sample contract and how to interpret its findings at a high level. By the end, you should understand why audits combine human expertise with automation, where formal proofs fit, and what to insist on when planning an audit for a real project. Consider this chapter your playbook for turning a codebase into an auditable, durable deployment.

screens.title: Why Audits Matter
screens.narratorSegment: Audits matter because once code lives on-chain, changes are hard or impossible. That immutability means a bug can lock funds, allow theft, or break core functionality with no easy rollback. An audit is a structured effort to find and fix issues while the code is still mutable, or to design upgrade mechanisms that themselves are secure. Consider the practical cost: migrating to a patched contract requires carefully transferring state and users, a process that is expensive and introduces risk. Audits reduce those risks by catching subtle logic errors and edge cases that tests and automated scanners alone may miss. A focused manual review inspects business logic and component interactions; automated tools surface common anti-patterns quickly; and formal verification mathematically proves properties for the smallest critical pieces. A misconception to avoid is thinking that automated tools are sufficient: they find many problems but miss interactions and novel attacks. Your takeaway is simple: prioritize auditing early and allocate time for human-led analysis — this is the primary way to avoid irreversible operational and financial damage. Why Audits Matter means an audit is a proactive, structured security review that reduces risk before code is deployed to an immutable ledger.. In practical terms, the immutability problem and the cost of post-deployment fixes. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › Why Audits Matter
Why audits are essential
Immutable deployments and irreversible financial impact demand pre-deployment assurance.
Definition
A systematic review to find security and logical flaws before deployment.
Why it matters
  • Immutable contracts make fixes expensive and risky.
  • Small logic errors can lead to large financial losses.
  • Audits preserve user trust and project reputation.
Concrete Example
A contract with an access-control mistake can let any caller change ownership or drain funds; an audit finds the missing check before deployment.
Common misconception
Relying solely on automated tools will miss subtle business logic interactions that only a human review reveals.
Key Takeaway

Treat auditing as insurance: design your development timeline so audits complete before final deployment and include re-audits after fixes.

Audit roles and methods
Automated tools — quick scans for known patterns like reentrancy and integer issues.
Manual review — deep inspection of business logic and interactions between contracts.
Formal verification — mathematical proofs for critical properties on small, critical components.
Why combine methods?
Automated tools provide breadth, manual review provides depth, and formal verification provides the highest assurance for critical invariants. Together they reduce different classes of risk.

screens.title: Manual Review vs Automated Tools vs Formal Verification
screens.narratorSegment: There are three complementary audit approaches. Manual review is human-driven: experienced auditors read the code, check design documents, and reason about interactions and business logic. This approach excels at catching subtle logic flaws, integration mismatches, and novel attack patterns. However, it is time-consuming and depends on auditor expertise. Automated tools like Slither and Mythril scan code fast and consistently, surfacing known anti-patterns such as reentrancy or unchecked arithmetic. They are efficient for baseline hygiene and continuous integration, but they rely on pattern matching and produce false positives or miss new attack types. Formal verification uses mathematical models to prove properties about code; it's the highest assurance level for critical invariants but is expensive and usually applied only to small, essential modules. A common misconception is assuming formal verification replaces testing; instead, it complements tests by providing proof for specific properties while tests exercise behavior. In practice, combine all three: use scanners to find obvious issues, manual reviewers to analyze design and edge cases, and formal methods for the smallest critical components that require near-total certainty. Manual Review vs Automated Tools vs Formal Verification means each method addresses different risks: automated tools for breadth, manual review for depth, and formal verification for critical certainty.. In practical terms, strengths, limits, and when to apply each method. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › Manual vs Automated vs Formal
Manual Code Review
Human auditors inspect code line by line, compare implementations to specifications, and reason about business logic and complex interactions.
  • Strength: catches design and logic errors.
  • Limit: time-intensive and expertise-dependent.
  • Example: spotting cross-contract interaction flaws.
Automated Tools
Tools like Slither, Mythril, and Truffle Security quickly flag known patterns, enabling broad coverage and CI integration.
  • Strength: speed and repeatability.
  • Limit: false positives, pattern-limited detection.
  • Example: detecting reentrancy or integer issues at scale.
Formal Verification
Mathematical proofs show that specified properties always hold, offering the highest assurance for critical code paths.
  • Strength: near-absolute assurance for proved properties.
  • Limit: high cost and best for small, critical modules.
  • Example: proving only the owner can withdraw funds under all inputs.
Practical combination
Use automated tools for breadth, manual review for design and interaction analysis, and formal verification for the small properties where failure is unacceptable.

screens.title: Typical Audit Phases
screens.narratorSegment: A comprehensive audit proceeds in defined phases that make the work traceable and effective. Start with scope definition and information gathering: the audit team collaborates with developers to understand intended behavior, the architecture, and threat models. This reduces wasted effort and sets expectations. Next run an initial automated analysis using tools to find obvious issues quickly. Then move into the intensive manual review where auditors examine code, write tests that aim to break the contract, and reason about edge cases. When vulnerabilities are identified, categorize them by severity and prepare a clear report that explains the issue, demonstrates exploitability where relevant, and recommends concrete remediation. After the development team fixes issues, perform a remediation verification or re-audit to confirm fixes and check for regressions. A common mistake is skipping the re-audit; assuming fixes are correct leaves projects exposed. Treat the timeline as iterative: scope and documentation evolve, and critical fixes may trigger a focused re-review. This structure helps teams allocate resources and avoid last-minute surprises. Typical Audit Phases means follow scope, scan, manual review, report, remediate, and re-audit to ensure issues are found and correctly fixed before deployment.. In practical terms, from scoping to re-audit: a practical timeline you can follow. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › Typical Audit Phases
Audit timeline and phases
Scope definition & information gathering
Collect specs, whitepapers, and test suites. Define assets, critical functions, and threat models to focus the audit.
Initial automated analysis
Run scanners to find low-hanging fruit and prepare a list of warnings to prioritize for manual review.
Manual code review and vulnerability identification
Auditors inspect logic, write exploit-oriented tests, and identify severity-ranked issues with reproduction steps.
Reporting, remediation, and re-audit
Deliver a clear report, the team remediates, and auditors re-check fixes during a re-audit to close the loop.
Example deliverable
A findings spreadsheet with severity, reproduction steps, remediation suggestions, and status per issue.
Common mistake
Skipping the re-audit. Fixes can introduce regressions; a follow-up review is essential to confirm safety.
Pro tip
Define critical properties early so manual review and any formal verification focus on core invariants.

screens.narratorSegment: This screen walks through using a static analyzer on an example contract. You will not only run the tool but also learn how to triage its output. The sample contract contains common patterns that may trigger warnings: public owner setter, external calls in a withdrawal flow, and a balances mapping. First, save the provided Solidity file and run the analyzer. The tool will flag patterns like potential reentrancy or missing access checks. When you read the report, remember that a flagged pattern is a hypothesis: auditors manually inspect the code to confirm exploitability, add context, and write tests that try to reproduce the issue. For example, if a transfer is executed before state is updated, an auditor will attempt to create a reentrancy test case to verify whether funds can be drained. Also be mindful of false positives: modern Solidity versions prevent certain integer underflows, but legacy patterns may still be pointed out. content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › Simulating an Audit with Slither
Run the analyzer
Save the following file as AuditMe.sol and run the analyzer (for example using the command suggested by your tool). Use the tool's output to create hypotheses that you will then confirm or refute with manual inspection and tests.
// SPDX-License-Identifier: MIT
pragma solidity ^0.8.0;

contract AuditMe {
    address public owner;
    mapping(address => uint) public balances;

    constructor() {
        owner = msg.sender;
    }

    function deposit() public payable {
        balances[msg.sender] += msg.value;
    }

    function withdraw(uint _amount) public {
        require(balances[msg.sender] >= _amount, "Insufficient balance");

        (bool success, ) = payable(msg.sender).call{value: _amount}("");
        require(success, "Transfer failed");

        balances[msg.sender] -= _amount;
    }

    function getBalance() public view returns (uint) {
        return address(this).balance;
    }

    function setOwner(address _newOwner) public {
        owner = _newOwner;
    }
}
How to interpret findings
  • Treat tool warnings as hypotheses for manual review and targeted tests.
  • Differentiate between language-level protections and logical vulnerabilities.
  • Confirm exploitability with a focused unit or integration test before labeling severity as critical.
Concrete example
If the tool flags the withdraw flow as potentially reentrant, write a test that performs a reentrancy attempt and verify whether state updates happen in the safe order.
Key Takeaway

Automated scans speed discovery, but human reasoning and tests determine real exploit risk and remediation priority.

screens.title: Vulnerability Types and Severity
screens.narratorSegment: Auditors group vulnerabilities by type and severity to help teams prioritize remediation. Typical classes include reentrancy, access-control flaws, input validation failures, integer arithmetic issues, and gas-related problems. Each class has a different likelihood and impact profile. Severity is usually categorized as critical, high, medium, low, and informational. A critical finding might allow immediate theft of funds or permanent loss of assets; a high issue could lead to serious misbehavior under specific conditions; medium and low are less likely to be exploitable or easier to fix. When you read a report, look for exploitability proof, reproduction steps, and suggested fixes. A common trap is focusing on lower-severity items while leaving a single critical logic flaw unaddressed. Auditors provide a hierarchy to direct attention: fix critical and high issues first, then address medium and low findings. The practical skill is to evaluate whether suggested fixes change other behaviors and to require a re-audit for any significant change. content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › Vulnerability Types & Severity
Common vulnerability types
  • Reentrancy — external calls that allow reentry into a contract before state updates complete.
  • Access control — missing or incorrect ownership and authorization checks.
  • Input validation — unchecked external inputs or assumptions about callers.
  • Integer and arithmetic — overflow/underflow or incorrect assumptions about limits.
  • Gas and logic — functions that can fail unexpectedly due to gas or ordering issues.
Concrete example
A withdraw function that executes an external call before updating user balances can be exploited in a reentrancy attack to withdraw repeatedly, draining funds.
Severity classification
Auditors rank findings as critical, high, medium, low, or informational based on exploitability and impact. Reports should justify the rank and provide reproduction steps.
  • Critical: immediate fund loss or permanent corruption.
  • High: serious break under plausible conditions.
  • Medium/Low: less likely or easier to mitigate.
Common mistake
Treating all automated warnings as equally urgent; instead, use severity and exploitability tests to prioritize fixes.
Key Takeaway

Use severity and exploitability together: fix critical and high issues first and verify fixes with a re-audit.

screens.title: Lessons from Historical Hacks
screens.narratorSegment: Historical incidents teach auditors where to focus. The DAO incident highlights reentrancy patterns that can drain funds when state updates occur after external calls. The Parity multi-sig issue shows how access-control flaws and mistaken ownership changes can freeze funds irreversibly. The Wormhole bridge incident illustrates the danger of inadequate input validation and assumptions about external components, allowing unauthorized minting. Each case demonstrates that small, localized bugs can have system-wide financial consequences. screens.title: Reporting, Remediation, and Re-Audit
screens.narratorSegment: A good audit report clearly communicates findings, their severity, reproduction steps, and concrete remediation suggestions. Reports should make it easy for developers to act: include code references, minimal reproductions, and suggested code changes or defensive patterns. Severity ratings must be justified by exploitability and impact evidence. After remediation, a re-audit or verification pass confirms fixes and checks for regressions introduced by fixes. Skipping this step is a common and dangerous mistake. When you plan remediation, treat changes as potential new risk surfaces: a fix that centralizes privileges or adds upgradeability must itself be audited. screens.title: Developer Safety Notes and Preventive Design

fullNarratorScript:
Auditing smart contracts and blockchain systems is not an optional step; it's a fundamental safety practice. In an immutable environment, bugs become permanent unless you design costly migrations, so catching issues early protects funds, users, and reputation. In this lesson you will learn the three primary audit methodologies — manual review, automated scanning, and formal verification — how audits are staged from scoping to re-audit, and the common vulnerability patterns auditors look for. We'll connect these methods to concrete historical examples, like reentrancy and access-control errors, so you can see how a small flaw produced outsized loss. You will also get a practical orientation to running a static analyzer on a sample contract and how to interpret its findings at a high level. By the end, you should understand why audits combine human expertise with automation, where formal proofs fit, and what to insist on when planning an audit for a real project. Consider this chapter your playbook for turning a codebase into an auditable, durable deployment.

These objectives describe the concrete skills you will build. First, you will explain why auditing is essential for blockchains and smart contracts, including the practical consequences of skipping audits. For example, you will connect audit failures to real incidents where immutable ledgers compounded losses. Second, you will describe and contrast the main audit methodologies — manual review, automated tools, and formal verification — and say when each is appropriate. Third, you will outline the phases of a comprehensive audit from scoping and automated scans to reporting and re-audit, and explain why each phase matters. Finally, you will identify common classes of vulnerabilities and how auditors typically report them by severity so you can prioritize fixes. Each objective links a capability with a real-world reason: protecting funds, minimizing migration costs, and preserving project reputation. Keep these outcomes in mind as checkpoints when you review an audit plan or design your next smart contract release.

This second objectives slide focuses on practical skills you will practice. You will analyze audit reports to interpret severity classifications and prioritize remediation actions. You will learn how to run a static analyzer on a sample contract and interpret the tool's warnings versus true bugs. You will be able to design a re-audit plan to verify fixes and avoid the common mistake of skipping follow-up reviews. Finally, you will examine historical hacks to extract lessons that inform future audits, such as preferring battle-tested libraries and treating external inputs as untrusted. Each objective links to a measurable activity: reading reports, running Slither, designing re-audits, and summarizing incidents. These practical objectives prepare you to participate in or manage audits with clarity and to communicate security trade-offs to development and leadership teams. Learning Objectives — Practical Skills means apply scanners, interpret findings, design re-audits, and learn from past incidents to improve future audit outcomes.. In practical terms, hands-on and analysis-focused objectives you will practice. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Audits matter because once code lives on-chain, changes are hard or impossible. That immutability means a bug can lock funds, allow theft, or break core functionality with no easy rollback. An audit is a structured effort to find and fix issues while the code is still mutable, or to design upgrade mechanisms that themselves are secure. Consider the practical cost: migrating to a patched contract requires carefully transferring state and users, a process that is expensive and introduces risk. Audits reduce those risks by catching subtle logic errors and edge cases that tests and automated scanners alone may miss. A focused manual review inspects business logic and component interactions; automated tools surface common anti-patterns quickly; and formal verification mathematically proves properties for the smallest critical pieces. A misconception to avoid is thinking that automated tools are sufficient: they find many problems but miss interactions and novel attacks. Your takeaway is simple: prioritize auditing early and allocate time for human-led analysis — this is the primary way to avoid irreversible operational and financial damage. Why Audits Matter means an audit is a proactive, structured security review that reduces risk before code is deployed to an immutable ledger.. In practical terms, the immutability problem and the cost of post-deployment fixes. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

There are three complementary audit approaches. Manual review is human-driven: experienced auditors read the code, check design documents, and reason about interactions and business logic. This approach excels at catching subtle logic flaws, integration mismatches, and novel attack patterns. However, it is time-consuming and depends on auditor expertise. Automated tools like Slither and Mythril scan code fast and consistently, surfacing known anti-patterns such as reentrancy or unchecked arithmetic. They are efficient for baseline hygiene and continuous integration, but they rely on pattern matching and produce false positives or miss new attack types. Formal verification uses mathematical models to prove properties about code; it's the highest assurance level for critical invariants but is expensive and usually applied only to small, essential modules. A common misconception is assuming formal verification replaces testing; instead, it complements tests by providing proof for specific properties while tests exercise behavior. In practice, combine all three: use scanners to find obvious issues, manual reviewers to analyze design and edge cases, and formal methods for the smallest critical components that require near-total certainty. This reduces wasted effort and sets expectations. Next run an initial automated analysis using tools to find obvious issues quickly. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.
